aliases.description: Other part numbers / names for the same device (vendor prefixes, package suffixes). Name references elsewhere (a controller's outputs.driver.IC) resolve against name and aliases.

manufacturers.description: Companies that build it, when they differ from the creator

price.description: Single price (USD unless {amount, currency}) or published quantity tiers

direction.description: fixed: one way, input to output (buffers, drivers). dir-pin: either way, set by a DIR input (bus transceivers). auto: senses the direction itself (auto-direction translators, weak drive).

buffered.description: Whether the outputs are strong enough to drive a cable to the pixels. true for bus buffers and line drivers. false for translators made for short links between chips, whose outputs are held through a resistor: pass-gate parts with pull-ups (TXS010x), auto-direction parts with a series resistor on each output (TXB010x, whatever the maker calls the architecture), MOSFET or resistor shifters.

differential.description: Differential signalling (RS-485-style pairs) on the input side: a line receiver, not a logic-level buffer

packages.description: Every package the part comes in (common.json ic_package); pin counts come from the names

supply_voltage.description: Supply voltage (VCC) the part runs from, usually a range ('1.65-5.5V')

max_voltage.description: Highest voltage it takes, for boards whose supply range isn't published (ICs use supply_voltage)

input_high_voltage.description: Lowest input voltage guaranteed to read as high (the datasheet's VIH min) when the part is powered to output 5 V; for dual-supply parts, with the input side on the controller's 3.3 V rail. A 3.3 V controller can only drive the part when this is below 3.3 V. Put the datasheet's test condition in input_high_voltage_notes.
